payload.original: Historical investigation recorded from primary sources. During the Plugs-Out Integrated Test of spacecraft 012 at Launch Complex 34 on 27 January 1967, a fire in the 100-percent oxygen cabin killed the crew; the first crew report of fire began at 23:31:04.7 GMT [A1-C001, A1-C006, A1-C011]. Scope: ignition, fire progression, cabin atmosphere, combustibles, escape, emergency response, and corrective actions, distinguishing established conditions from the unproven exact ignition source.
payload.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Command Module fire, 27 January 1967

payload.original: Spacecraft 012 was mated to the launch vehicle at Launch Complex 34 on 6 January 1967. [A1-C002]
Spacecraft 012 was undergoing a "Plugs Out Integrated Test" (procedure OCP FO-K-0021-1) at the time of the accident on 27 January 1967. [A1-C001]
Crew positions: Grissom was command pilot (left seat), White senior pilot (middle seat), Chaffee pilot (right seat). [A1-C003]
The Plugs-Out Test began at 12:55 GMT (7:55 a.m. EST) when power was applied to the spacecraft. [A1-C008]
After hatch installation at 19:42 GMT, a cabin purge with oxygen began at 19:45 GMT. [A1-C007]
A significant voltage transient (surge in AC Bus 2 voltage) was recorded at 23:30:54.8 GMT. [A1-C009]
Finding 1a: there was a momentary power failure at 23:30:55 GMT. [A1-C010]
The first crew report of fire began at 23:31:04.7 GMT (6:31:04.7 p.m. EST). [A1-C011]
The fire was not intense until about 23:31:12 GMT; the slow early build-up is consistent with ignition in a zone with little combustible material. [A1-C014]
The cabin ruptured at about 23:31:19 GMT at a pressure of at least 29 psia. [A1-C015]
All transmission of voice and data from the spacecraft terminated by 23:31:22.4 GMT, three seconds after rupture. [A1-C017]
The Board estimated (an estimate, not an observation) that the Command Module atmosphere was lethal by 23:31:30 GMT, five seconds after the start of the third stage. [A1-C018]
All hatches were opened and the two outer hatches removed about five minutes after the fire report, at about 23:36 GMT (Pad Leader report ~5 min 27 s after first fire report). [A1-C022]
Later medical opinion based on autopsy concluded that resuscitation was impossible by 23:36 GMT (an upper bound inferred after the event, not an observation at 23:36). [A1-C023]
The doctors estimated their arrival at the White Room at 23:45 GMT; medical support was reported available at about 23:43 GMT. [A1-C024]

payload.mechanism: Pure oxygen at above-ambient pressure makes common materials burn intensely (Finding 9, A1-C057); nylon Raschel netting, Velcro and polyurethane foam carried the flame (A1-C025 to A1-C027); the pressure rise ruptured the cabin at a pressure of at least 29 psia (A1-C015). This catalog assigns the root-cause role to this combined hazardous condition; the Board itself lists six conditions without ranking a root cause (A1-C064).
payload.statement: The sealed Command Module cabin, pressurized with 100-percent oxygen at 16.7 psia and containing extensive combustible materials near possible ignition sources, turned a minor ignition into a rapidly fatal fire.

payload.mechanism: Board conclusion and Determination 1 (A1-C029, A1-C031) and Finding 1c (A1-C030). The initiation 'probably coincides' with the 23:30:55 GMT power interruption (A1-C034), but the Board cautions the transients may as easily be an effect of the fire (A1-C036). Overloaded conductors were examined and a few cases could not be exonerated completely (A1-C114). This is a most-probable determination, not a proven mechanism.
payload.statement: The fire was most probably brought about by a minor electrical malfunction or failure of equipment or wire insulation, the Board's most probable initiator being an electrical arc in the lower forward left-hand equipment bay near the Environmental Control Unit; the exact source was not identified.
The specific ignition source was a chafed power cable beneath the lithium hydroxide access door.
The specific ignition source was an arc at the cover of junction box C-15-1A-52 in the extreme lower-left corner of the lower equipment bay.
Spilled water/glycol coolant initiated the fire.
The fire was initiated non-electrically: electrostatic discharge, spontaneous combustion, mechanically produced heat or a struck object.
A malfunction of an electrically powered spacecraft system or subassembly initiated the fire.
The fire was caused by sabotage.

Deficiencies in Command Module design, workmanship and quality control, including vulnerable Teflon-insulated wiring and coolant plumbing, created multiple credible ignition opportunities (two of the three candidate arcs showed poor engineering and installation) and an unnecessarily hazardous condition.
The inward-opening, multi-piece hatch could not be opened against the cabin pressure, so the crew could not escape.

The test was not classified as hazardous, so no emergency escape, rescue, fire or medical preparations were in place; this contributed to the failed rescue, although in medical opinion the crew could not have been resuscitated by the time the hatches were opened.

payload.mechanism: Pre-fire knowledge and design rationale as stated by the Senate committee (A1-C108 to A1-C112): these were deliberate risk trade-offs made at the time, not neglect; recorded to avoid judging 1966 decisions only with 1967 hindsight.
payload.statement: The pure-oxygen fire hazard was known before the fire, and NASA chose to manage it by eliminating ignition sources; that strategy shaped the decisions not to fit a quick-opening hatch or a cabin extinguisher and not to treat the test as hazardous.

Program management problems (engineering orders open at delivery, an incomplete pre-test constraint list, insufficient response to changing program requirements) let deficiencies stand; the Senate committee inferred overconfidence from earlier pure-oxygen success.

payload.mechanism: A minor electrical fault, most probably an arc near the ECU (trigger; most probable, exact source unidentified), ignited combustibles in a sealed 100-percent oxygen cabin at 16.7 psia (root condition, as assigned by this catalog); the fire spread rapidly, the pressure rise ruptured the cabin at at least 29 psia about 15 s after the first crew report (about 24 s after the 23:30:55 transient) and toxic gases killed the crew. The inward-opening hatch prevented escape; the absence of rescue preparations for a test not classified as hazardous contributed to the failed rescue; deficient wiring and workmanship created credible ignition opportunities. Management problems and an ignition-elimination strategy, a deliberate pre-fire trade-off, let these conditions stand (enabling conditions).

payload.description: Remove the conditions for a rapid cabin fire: 60/40 oxygen-nitrogen launch-pad cabin atmosphere, restriction and control of combustible materials with material substitution, protective covers over wire bundles, stainless-steel oxygen lines and armored coolant solder joints.

Classify all tests in 100-percent oxygen environments as hazardous, establish an Office of Flight Safety independent of the program office, and provide emergency procedures, equipment and training for pad tests.

payload.statement: Sources give the pre-fire launch-pad cabin pressure as 16.5 psia (TN D-5654) and 16.7 psia (Review Board).

payload.statement: The Apollo 7 launch cabin atmosphere was measured at about 64/36 oxygen-nitrogen, against the nominal 60/40.

payload.residualUncertainty: The exact ignition source remains unknown and probably unknowable: several candidate arcs exist and the evidence was destroyed; whether the 23:30:55 GMT power transient was cause or effect is undetermined. The root-cause role for the oxygen-and-combustibles condition is this catalog's assignment, not the Board's ranking. The fire tests that verify the atmosphere change are the same series that selected it, and circuit-breaker panels were accepted rather than corrected; Apollo 7 is corroboration, not a fire test. The test-safety measures are documented only by a Senate summary. The unified hatch's opening time has not been verified from a retrieved primary record (requirements, qualification tests and flight use are documented, measured times are not), so the hatch correction remains awaiting verification and the investigation is not resolved. Pre-fire decisions (no quick hatch, no extinguisher, test not hazardous) were deliberate trade-offs under an ignition-elimination strategy.
payload.statement: The Apollo 1 crew died in a fire that spread rapidly through a sealed 100-percent oxygen cabin at 16.7 psia containing extensive combustibles; the fire was most probably ignited by an electrical arc from vulnerable wiring near the Environmental Control Unit, but the exact ignition source was not identified. The inward-opening hatch could not be opened against cabin pressure and the test had not been treated as hazardous. Full-scale mock-up fire tests found the revised atmosphere and materials firesafe, conditional on minor material changes, and Apollo 7 flew the changed spacecraft with its systems operating as intended almost without exception.
